recommended_title: Local Residual Scaling for Compositional Conformal Prediction: Benefits and Limits
central_question: When does training-only local residual scaling improve the coverage–reference-mass tradeoff of split-conformal regions for continuous compositions, and what do homoscedastic and covariate-shift controls reveal about its limits?
central_thesis: In the evaluated logistic-normal settings, the frozen training-only scale-selection procedure improves measured coverage–reference-mass tradeoffs over global ILR calibration under boundary-concentrated heteroscedasticity, provides no consistent homoscedastic advantage, and performs favorably under the tested shift without establishing shifted-distribution validity or a contribution attributable specifically to quantile stumps.
narrative_rationale: This is a controlled empirical study of a positive scale function inside a fixed compositional conformal construction, not a new geometry, universal reliability guarantee, or search-success narrative. Six final seed episodes provide matched global-ILR, raw-simplex and Bonferroni comparisons, two nominal levels, fixed subgroups, reference-mass estimates, controls, and paired aggregate uncertainty. The strong contrast between homoscedastic and boundary-concentrated heteroscedastic conditions supplies a coherent scientific question; shifted cases supply a limited stress test rather than another validity theorem. Direct source inspection identifies a complete ridge/constant/tail-blend selection procedure, but no selected-component diagnostics or matched final ridge-only comparison. Conditional empirical benefits therefore beat both a universal-superiority story and an unsupported stump-specific mechanism story. A latent-count bridge was not implemented and an interaction extension has no usable performance evidence. Publication-worthiness is a framing judgment, not an additional qualification result.

These change the research scope from generic classifier probabilities to continuous simplex-valued responses.

The original quadratic-feature ridge scale is available as code and search context, but not as a matched repeated-final comparator. Do not substitute the global-ILR baseline for it or compare its search score to final scores. No study.* sources exist here, so do not report selection deltas or scored/unscored attempt counts as study-grounded findings.

method_groups.name: Training-only local scale selection in ILR space
method_groups.include_reason: The frozen evaluated procedure selects among a quadratic-feature ridge log-scale, a constant, and four ridge/tail log-space blends using three training folds, fitting-only alignment, and a one-standard-error heuristic. Describe and evaluate the entire procedure, not a proven quantile-stump winner.

method_groups.name: Global ILR split conformal
method_groups.include_reason: Primary matched comparator: same training-only ridge center, ILR Euclidean residual geometry, calibration split and corrected rank, without covariate-dependent scaling. It isolates scale adaptivity more cleanly than cross-geometry comparisons and is not the original ridge-scale implementation.

method_groups.name: Raw-simplex L-infinity split conformal
method_groups.include_reason: Grounded alternative representation and region shape, evaluated on the same target compositions, splits, centers and reference probes. It contextualizes the ILR comparison without claiming geometry is independently ablated.

method_groups.name: Coordinatewise Bonferroni regions
method_groups.include_reason: Grounded simultaneous-coordinate comparator using corrected per-coordinate calibration at alpha divided by dimension; expose its coverage and reference-mass tradeoffs rather than reducing comparison to one aggregate score.

method_groups.name: Constant-scale and permuted-residual controls
method_groups.include_reason: Training controls examine scale invariance and the dependence on covariate–residual alignment. Constant scale numerically reproduces global ILR; do not plot it as another independent baseline. Permuted residuals support an alignment interpretation but do not isolate stumps, blend weights, or the selection rule.

method_groups.name: Calibration and degenerate-region sanity comparators
method_groups.include_reason: Uncalibrated residual quantiles, the full simplex and a singleton center are available for supplementary checks of coverage–mass interpretation. They are not competing learned methods and need not dominate the main narrative.

results_focus: Main comparison: four scientifically meaningful methods, grouped by homoscedastic (H), boundary-concentrated heteroscedastic (B), and shifted heteroscedastic (S) conditions, with dimension 3 versus 10 treated as adaptations under one thesis rather than independent experiments.

Show coverage at nominal 0.95 and 0.90 separately, not only absolute errors. Show reference mass separately from coverage so that an apparently small region cannot hide undercoverage. Efficiency is probability mass under the fixed mixed probe distribution, not geometric volume, expected cardinality, or a distribution-free quantity.

Keep fixed-subgroup evidence in the main paper: a compact six-condition table compares the local procedure, global ILR and permuted-residual control using mean absolute subgroup coverage error over both groups and both levels. Supporting tables retain the signed per-group, per-level coverage and per-seed Wilson intervals; empirical group diagnostics are not conditional guarantees.

Homoscedastic cases show little benefit and small aggregate-utility disadvantages relative to global ILR; do not omit them. Boundary heteroscedastic cases support the strongest joint subgroup-error/reference-mass comparison. Boundary concentration and heteroscedasticity change together, so neither factor is independently causally identified.

Shifted cases have favorable observed coverage relative to the matched global comparator, but exchangeability is not supplied by the unweighted algorithm. In shifted dimension 3 the local method has larger reference mass than global ILR, so do not claim uniformly smaller regions or a free efficiency gain.

An aggregate main-text table may report mean utility 0.8772268474776957 with its stored 95% seed-bootstrap interval [0.8766236679621646, 0.8781275287778212], mean marginal absolute coverage error 0.011729600694444453, mean fixed-group absolute coverage error 0.015105333854689552, and reference mass 0.4508402082655165, with sensible rounding. Sources: final.metric.* entries with matching names. Define utility from evaluator code as 1 - [0.375 marginal error + 0.375 group error + 0.25 reference mass]; it is a chosen evaluation weighting, not universal reliability.

The aggregate local-minus-global utility difference is 0.04762325792650014 (final.metric.global_ilr_score_gap); its stored paired six-seed bootstrap interval is [0.043901240346666696, 0.050616967867983816] (final.evidence.episodes). Interpret it as a fixed-six-case aggregate, not evidence of per-case superiority or proof that stumps improve the original ridge-scale method.

Final uncertainty uses six seeds [1009, 2003, 3001, 4001, 5003, 6007] and stored 2000-resample paired seed-bootstrap intervals. Repeated copies of the same aggregate interval inside episodes are one estimate, not six independent estimates. Coverage Wilson intervals describe within-seed test hits; do not average interval endpoints or use a mass Wilson interval as an independent-query population interval.
figure_plan: Figure 1, early conceptual overview: interior-simplex response -> ILR center and training-only positive scale -> held-out normalized-score calibration -> separate coverage, subgroup and reference-mass evaluation; mark the shifted condition outside the exchangeability guarantee.

Figure 2, main reliability comparison: four panels in a 2-by-2 grid for dimension and nominal level, comparing the four main methods across H/B/S with all six seed points and an arithmetic-mean marker. Nominal coverage is a horizontal line, not an attainment-rate label.

Figure 3, companion efficiency comparison: two dimension panels comparing reference mass across H/B/S and the same four methods, explicitly averaged over the two nominal levels within each seed. Read alongside Figure 2 and the main subgroup table, never as a standalone superiority ranking.

figure_specs.layout_rationale: Use the full 5.5-inch single-column width, approximately 4.2 inches high, about 0.55 page including caption. figure_specs.layout_rationale: Target 5.5 by 2.5 inches across two side-by-side panels, about 0.35 page including caption. planned_subsections.heading: Complete Conditional Scale-Selection Specification
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Use the inspected selected program and METHOD.md for the quadratic ridge features, tail target 0.9, 15 candidate threshold quantiles, minimum leaf size, learning rate 0.1, maximum 80 stump updates, three deterministic folds, constant and four log blends, fitting-only alignment, simplicity ordering, all-data refit, scale floors and evaluator clipping. Explain that the one-standard-error rule is a heuristic, not a significance test. Include pseudocode derived from source, not selected-component frequencies that were never recorded. Final evidence binds the evaluated method; source linkage is documentary unless independently verified later.

planned_subsections.heading: Generator, Splits, Geometry and Reference Measure
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Document task/evaluate_final.py and task/resources/final/manifest.json: six-dimensional Gaussian covariates; H/B/S generator equations; dimension 3/10; center-fit, scale-fit, calibration and test sizes 1024/1024/512/2048; the test first-covariate shift 1.25; shared ridge center; exact ILR basis; strictly positive responses; 128 selected test covariates and 1024 probes per query from a half Gaussian-in-ILR/half uniform-simplex mixture. Explain query clustering, data-dependent reference covariance, and why mass is not geometric volume. No exact-zero, finite-count or real-data experiment is implied.

planned_subsections.heading: Full Seed-Level Coverage and Efficiency Tables
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Tabulate all final cases and seeds, both alphas, both fixed sign-of-first-covariate groups, all four main methods, and available within-seed Wilson intervals. Retain signed coverage deviations as well as absolute errors and reference mass; do not infer general conditional coverage. Show stored aggregate paired intervals once and describe the fixed-case, seed-resampling unit. Tables can be generated solely from the final.evidence.episodes pointer.

planned_subsections.heading: Alignment, Calibration and Degenerate-Region Checks
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Report constant/global numerical agreement, permuted-training-residual results, uncalibrated residual-quantile baseline, full-simplex and singleton-center coverage/mass, using their stored final records. State what each check tests and cannot establish. Do not invent a stump-only, ridge-only, no-selection, interaction-depth, sample-size, dimension-sweep or weighted-shift ablation.

planned_subsections.heading: Conditional Rank Argument and Its Boundaries
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Give the standard split-conformal rank argument conditional on the center-fit and scale-fit data: a fixed positive scale preserves exchangeable calibration/test scores; k=ceil((m+1)(1-alpha)) with infinity for k>m gives marginal coverage under the stated assumptions. Cover ties and common clipping. Do not label it a new theorem, a group-coverage guarantee, or shifted-distribution validity; novelty and supporting citations need independent literature verification.

The shared reference distribution is a training-dependent mixture, not invariant simplex volume. Probe-hit Wilson intervals are evaluator-provided binomial-style summaries over clustered query/probe hits; they do not quantify all query-sampling uncertainty. Six seeds and a fixed condition grid limit bootstrap precision and external validity. Do not pool all test examples across seeds as if one independently fitted model generated them.

Do not equate composition-region coverage with class-label prediction-set coverage, calibration of class probabilities, latent multinomial-probability recovery, or true conditional-probability identification. Outputs here are strictly positive continuous logistic-normal responses, not softmax predictions from an evaluated classifier, exact-zero compositions, CIFAR data or finite-count observations.
